chapters.matn:
Routes crossing the Sahara linked the Middle Niger with North African markets. Merchants moved salt, metals, textiles and other goods through settlements whose rulers and households did not share one form of religious life. Muslim traders, literate officials and teachers could live at courts where many subjects continued different practices. Mali's royal power and Mansa Mūsā's pilgrimage in 1324 connected West African political prestige with wider Islamic centres, but royal pilgrimage did not by itself determine the religious understanding of every village.

Under later Songhay rule, Timbuktu and Jenne supported merchants, jurists, teachers and families who collected and copied books. Scholarship required more than a ruler's patronage. Students learned from named authorities, debated cases arising from local marriages, property and exchange, and preserved memories of teachers whose credibility did not depend wholly upon office. Writers such as Aḥmad Bābā participated in wider Mālikī discussions while responding to the histories of their own towns.

The resulting Islamic culture was neither simply imported from Cairo nor entirely independent of transregional texts. Local languages, commerce, learned households and relations with rulers gave inherited disciplines distinctive forms. Spiritual guidance could be received through actual teaching and companionship while political authority remained contested. The moral life of the community therefore depended upon interactions among merchants, scholars, rulers and families, not on a claim that the mere possession of Arabic manuscripts made everyone realized.
chapters.sharh_add:
The Middle Niger offers a strong test of the difference between a shared revealed orientation and the geographical replication of one imperial institution. A student in Timbuktu could study Mālikī law and Arabic grammar within familial teaching relations and local patterns of commerce very different from those of a Cairo college. Historical evidence must identify the actual teacher, book, ownership record or surviving biography. A library catalogue documents material survival and circulation; it does not reveal the spiritual station of its owner.

The merchant's place is equally important. Trust in credit, shelter along a journey and repeated exchange can make a town able to sustain scribes and teachers, but commercial contact does not automatically produce conversion or a spiritual discipline. Such changes require people who teach, listen, imitate and acquire recognizable habits. Royal patronage, meanwhile, can support a mosque or court and can also threaten scholarly independence when public judgment opposes powerful interests.

Aḥmad Bābā's later career and Moroccan intervention make these tensions concrete. Learned authority could survive political upheaval through manuscripts and students, while actual families suffered loss or displacement. The Akbarian idea of Muhammadan comprehensiveness provides a standard for relating partial goods—commerce, law, teaching, worship—without treating all West African religious practices as fully formed instances of one metaphysical station.

The evidence remains uneven. The *Tārīkh al-Sūdān*, travellers' narratives, scholarly biographical writings and archaeological materials must not be flattened into one chronology. Manuscript collections vary widely in age and provenance, so the historical claim is local and document-dependent: real African communities produced and transmitted Islamic learning in their own distinct social settings.

chapters.matn:
Merchants and sailors travelled the Indian Ocean by the seasonal winds, crossing between East Africa, the Arabian shores, India and Southeast Asia. Traders of different religions shared ports where lodging, credit, weights, protection and trusted interpreters could affect the success of a voyage. Some travellers remained in settlements, formed households through marriage and established places of worship and instruction. Children born into these communities learned local languages and participated in maritime economies without ceasing to belong to wider religious networks.

By the fifteenth century Melaka had become a major port whose rulers governed resident and temporary merchants through harbour arrangements, customs and protection. Its commercial life involved Chinese, Indian and island Southeast Asian networks as well as Muslim ones. Malay religious instruction and literature developed through locally teachable forms, including Arabic-derived writing, learned travel and the work of translators and jurists. The date of particular rulers' conversions and the sequence of local changes remain disputed.

Islamic practice spread through persons, repeated relationships and public institutions rather than a single migrating administrative model. A commercial promise could prepare a relationship of trust; a teacher could give that relationship religious direction; a household could transmit practice across generations. Yet trade itself did not prove sanctity, and Muslim court identity did not establish that every inhabitant followed the same law. The common Prophetic inheritance took historically differentiated forms through sea, language and domestic life.
chapters.sharh_add:
In Melaka, the *syahbandar* and harbour customs help identify the practical causes that brought different people into sustained contact. A visiting merchant needed protection and predictable dealings; a resident family needed continuity through seasons when ships departed; a teacher needed a language in which students could understand instruction. These functions could support one another without any one being reducible to the others. Historical research by Kenneth Hall and A. C. S. Peacock distinguishes harbour administration, trade, Arabic and Persian knowledge and local Southeast Asian sources.

The micro-to-macro pathway is especially clear: one marriage forms responsibilities between people; a recurring neighbourhood of merchants and families establishes repeated worship; learners can acquire ritual and ethical *malakāt* from teachers; scribes and patrons then make such practices portable through manuscripts. Every arrow requires real history. It is a hypothesis, not a claim that every documented Malay community developed by an identical sequence.

The vertical claim concerns the possibility that worship, honesty, hospitality, mutual support and spiritual education participate in one revealed orientation. It does not entail that importing a legal text automatically regenerates the Prophet's lived wholeness. A Malay scholar might be genuinely competent in law or devotion through a form of life very different from an Arabian town, while still requiring faithful interpretation of authoritative sources.

The precise conversion chronology of early Malay rulers remains disputed. Written Malay, Arabic, Persian and Portuguese accounts are not one transparent collective witness. Source evaluation must preserve distinct time periods and the difference between a court's public Islamic identity and the acquisition of religious practice by persons throughout the port.

chapters.matn:
In the eastern Bengal delta, waterways shifted while cultivators cleared fields and established new settlements. The spread of Muslim communities did not simply reproduce the path of earlier military conquest. Land grants, new village institutions, locally remembered religious figures and expanding agrarian work often moved together in particular districts. A family attached to a newly cultivated place could receive instruction and form devotional habits through a remembered teacher or shrine without participating in one identifiable mass conversion.

Persianate administration and Muslim courts interacted with Bengali-speaking households, agricultural obligations and local traditions. A foundation associated with a religious figure might provide a mosque, support teachers or help organize cultivation, while carrying claims about land and authority that needed enforcement. The same place could possess a material, political and devotional significance without those meanings being interchangeable.

Over generations, prayer, family custom, religious education and local memory acquired recognizable continuities among communities living far from the earliest centres of Muslim political power. The acts of particular households constituted much of that continuity, while rivers, harvests and land tenure shaped their possibilities. The religious development of Bengal therefore involved living relations among land, labour, spiritual teachers and political power. The spiritual value attached to a saintly founder cannot be deduced from a land grant, but neither does the economic explanation of a settlement exhaust what later worshippers understood themselves to be doing.
chapters.sharh_add:
Richard Eaton's study of Bengal distinguishes political, agrarian and religious frontiers, and in later work also describes other related historical movements. The central evidence includes dated inscriptions, settlement patterns, land grants and literary memories. A historian must ask which sources actually identify an event and which project later religious continuity backwards. One grant may establish property rights without specifying the religious convictions of the families cultivating it.

The religious teacher or saintly household becomes intelligible at the intermediate level. A follower may trust a teacher because of instruction, service, kin relations, perceived blessing or access to resources. These motives are not necessarily mutually exclusive; they also cannot be inferred with equal confidence from every record. The difference between *ṣuḥba*, practical support and spiritual realization must be retained. A person who visits a shrine is not thereby proved to have received the state attributed to its founder.

For the Akbarian frame, the land is a created good with real qualities, not merely a metaphor for a higher realm. A villager's work, household obligations and bodily prayer can become means of service when ordered toward appropriate ends. Yet the particular settlement's date and economic organization arise from water, soils, political authority and collective labour, not from a direct deduction of the divine Names.

The question of cultural difference also needs care. The appearance of Islamic practice in Bengali or Persian, or the coexistence of local customs with normative learning, does not automatically determine their correctness. The relevant jurists, teachers and worshippers interpreted them within actual disputes and habits. An integrated history must explain those decisions and why neighbouring villages could develop differently.

chapters.matn:
Ottoman rulers built an empire from an Anatolian principality, with Constantinople becoming the imperial capital after its conquest in 1453. Soldiers, tax officials, palace households and local intermediaries supported authority across the Balkans, Anatolia, the Arab provinces and the eastern Mediterranean. Mosques, courts, colleges and charitable endowments provided recurrent settings for worship, teaching and service among communities of different languages and religious affiliations.

Judges learned Ḥanafī legal doctrine while working alongside sultanic regulations concerning revenue and public administration. In a town, the court heard litigants whose disputes involved actual kin, debts, witnesses, trade and customary practices; a centrally issued order could address a different set of administrative concerns. Scholars gained office through increasingly organized educational appointments, but learned authority also persisted through households, private circles and Sufi networks that no court could fully control.

The Ottoman order made some forms of religious life and governance durable at large scale, yet none of its offices recreated the complete prophetic commission. A judge could issue a ruling, a ruler command an army, a teacher transmit knowledge and a shaykh guide students; their claims needed limits and mutual correction. The life of worship and character depended upon actual persons using institutions rightly. Different provinces developed different relations among imperial law, scholarly practice and local religious communities, making uniform political membership an insufficient measure of civilization.
chapters.sharh_add:
Ottoman institutions are an especially instructive case of specialization. A qāḍī's court, the *ʿilmiyye*, fiscal officers, Sufi lodges and family schools possessed different kinds of authority. Their relative integration was a historical achievement dependent upon appointments, training, documents, witnesses and particular rulers; it was not automatically secured by pronouncing the sultan the spiritual axis of society.

A court record preserves persons presenting specific claims and a judge's procedure; a sultanic *qānūn* shows a ruler's intended regulation. The two do not necessarily coincide in daily practice. Similarly, a madrasa credential attests a particular mode of scholarly achievement and authorization, not the possession of universal spiritual realization. Conversely, a shaykh's spiritual authority should not be treated as competence to set every tax or decide every title dispute.

Akbarian comprehensiveness supplies a normative limit, not a modern constitution or a doctrinal endorsement of every Ottoman institution. It asks whether each partial office acts in a relation appropriate to human and divine rights without claiming to be the whole. The outward durability of a mosque or endowment must be assessed alongside the quality of its teaching and the security of its beneficiaries.

Changes over centuries matter: the full sixteenth-century hierarchy should not be retrojected upon early fourteenth-century Anatolia. Annexation of older Arab scholarly regions brought further forms of local authority into the empire. The very possibility of common religious practice amid differing provincial arrangements is evidence against equating Muhammadan civilizational unity with one unchanging administrative form.

chapters.matn:
In early modern Iran the Safavid rulers made Twelver Shiʿism a defining public feature of their government, supported learned specialists and sought to alter the religious organization of communities whose practices had previously varied. The process took generations and occurred differently across provinces. Scholars arriving from established Imāmī centres taught law and doctrine, while political power, local institutions and religious attachments shaped the reception of their teaching.

Mughal rulers governed across India through military power, revenue arrangements, courtly Persian and negotiation with regional elites of diverse religions and languages. Akbar cultivated forms of discussion and imperial inclusion; later policies, including those under Aurangzeb, differed, with the compilation of major Ḥanafī legal materials among their learned projects. Jurists, philosophers, Sufi teachers, poets and learned households circulated works whose authority did not always coincide with a ruler's preference.

These empires did not express one interchangeable model of Islamic civilization. Safavid confessional policy, Mughal courtly discussion and Ottoman judicial institutions involved different relations between public power and religious scholarship. A subject could share a recognized legal tradition without sharing the political aims of its patrons. The material work of ruling and the inward formation of persons were interdependent but not identical, and the transmission of religious knowledge remained answerable to its sources even when dynasties supported it.
chapters.sharh_add:
The Safavid adoption of Shiʿi identity must be differentiated from the gradual formation of local institutions and personal practice. A ruler can order public symbols and sponsor teachers, yet the inward allegiance of families changes through schooling, marriage, liturgy, instruction and sometimes coercion over time. Twelver Shiʿi claims about the Imamate are not merely political preferences and must be represented in their own theological terms, while differing from Sunni and Akbarian accounts of *wilāya*.

The Mughal case demonstrates further plurality. Akbar's discussions and court policies were not identical to the apparatus collecting revenue, just as the *Fatāwā-yi ʿĀlamgīrī* was a scholarly compilation whose practical reception varied in place and period. The historian needs dated decrees, local records, texts and the work of actual jurists rather than a uniform characterization of “Mughal Islam.”

The spiritual and philosophical traditions of Safavid Iran and Mughal India were likewise not one discipline. Mullā Ṣadrā's metaphysics, Imāmī legal reasoning, Persian poetry, the work of Sufi lineages and South Asian hadith transmission interacted through specific people who sometimes disputed one another's claims. One cannot infer from their coexistence that they all endorsed the same theory of the Muhammadan Reality.

At the civilizational level the lesson is neither empty pluralism nor the assumption of a single standardized perfected order. A common orientation can be interpreted in contested ways and developed through institutions suited to different material conditions; their legitimacy must be argued from relevant sources and acts. No ruler, jurist or mystical author may be treated as reproducing the comprehensive Prophet ﷺ by possessing one fragment of his inheritance.
